newsitem.title: south koreA: N.Korean navy vessel intrudes into Southern waters.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean navy vessel intrudes into Southern waters.

text.p: A North Korean navy patrol boat intruded into Southern waters on Thursday, apparently by mistake as it shadowed a Chinese cargo ship, and stayed for almost an hour before returning, the South Korean defence ministry said.
A ministry official said it was the first such incursion since May 1996.
"The ship was first spotted at 2.05 p.m. (0505 GMT) and returned by 3.00 p.m.," the official said. "It seems that the ship mistakenly entered our waters."
He said the North Korean vessel appeared to be following a Chinese cargo vessel as it sailed south, but he gave no further details.
It was spotted just south of a nautical demarcation line, which has separated the two Koreas since a truce ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
Four South Korean navy vessels were immediately dispatched to the area, the official said. There was no contact with the North Korean boat.
Meanwhile, five North Korean defectors arrived at Seoul's international airport from an unidentified third country, television pictures showed.
They included the mother, a younger sister and a younger brother of a defector who arrived in January last year and who is now a student at Korea University.
The 49-year-old mother, Joo Young-hi, told reporters she had witnessed two to three people starve to death in her homeland every day.
"(Hunger) has ruined old women and children," Joo said. When asked how many people she had witnessed dying, she said: "Two to three every day."
The other two were a 25-year-old male college student and a 51-year-old man whose job was to earn hard currency for the military, a unification ministry statement said.
Last week, the first "boat people" defectors from North Korea also described people starving to death in their homeland during a press conference.

Fourteen members of two familes, who created a sensation early this month by becoming the first Northerners to flee to the South directly by sea, told the conference that life in the North was a constant battle to survive.
Growing numbers of North Koreans, stricken by chronic food shortages, have been seeking political asylum in the capitalist South.
Many escape through China and into Hong Kong, but that route is now threatened because of the imminent handover of the British colony to China.
